t.6.46.1: Then Prahasta, terrible and of terrible valor, marching forth roaring, his body enormous, surrounded by rākṣasas…
t.6.46.2: The great army of the mighty monkeys, their fury roused to the utmost, saw Prahasta as they roared at him.
t.6.46.4: And the wondrous bows, held firmly by the rākṣasas who longed for victory as they rushed against the vānaras, shone brilliantly.
t.6.46.3: Swords, javelins, lances and arrows, tridents and pestles, maces, iron clubs, barbed darts, and battle-axes of many kinds.
t.6.46.5: The bulls among the monkeys, those leaping creatures eager to fight, seized flowering trees and also huge, long rocks.
t.6.46.6: Having closed with one another, a very great battle arose among those many warriors as they rained down a shower of stones and a shower of arrows.
t.6.46.7: In that battle many rākṣasas slew many leaders of the vānara troops, and many vānaras too slew many rākṣasas.
t.6.46.8: Some were crushed by spears, and some by other excellent weapons; some were struck down with iron clubs, and some were cut apart by axes.
t.6.46.9: Some, again, lay fallen on the surface of the earth, breathless; others, their hearts pierced through, were bound fast by continuous streams of arrows.
t.6.46.10: Some of the vānaras, cut in two by swords, fell writhing upon the ground, and others were torn open at the flanks by the rākṣasas with their spears.
t.6.46.11: And on every side the hosts of rākṣasas were crushed upon the surface of the earth by the enraged monkeys with trees and mountain peaks.
t.6.46.13: In the battle there arose a tumultuous din from the monkeys and the rākṣasas, some crying out cries of pain and others roaring lion-like roars.
t.6.46.12: Struck violently by hands whose palms struck with the force of the thunderbolt, and by fists, they vomited blood from their mouths, their teeth and eyes shattered.
t.6.46.14: The enraged monkeys and rākṣasas, devoted to the path of heroes, fierce and with eyes rolling, performed their deeds as though without fear.
t.6.46.15: Narāntaka, Kumbhahanu, Mahānāda and Samunnata, these ministers of Prahasta, all struck down the forest-dwellers.
t.6.46.16: Of those who were swiftly rushing forward and slaying the Vānaras, Dvivida struck down one, Narāntaka, with a mountain peak.
t.6.46.18: But the mighty Jāmbavān, greatly enraged, seized a huge rock and hurled it down upon the chest of Mahānāda.
t.6.46.17: Then the monkey Durmukha, quick of hand, uprooted a huge tree and crushed the rākṣasa Samunnata with it.
t.6.46.20: Unable to endure that deed, Prahasta, mounted on his chariot with bow in hand, wrought a terrible slaughter of the forest-dwellers.
t.6.46.19: Then the valiant rākṣasa Kumbhahanu, attacked there by Tāra and struck on the head with a tree, gave up his life.
t.6.46.21: Then, in both armies, there arose something like a whirlpool, and a roar like that of the immeasurable ocean when it is agitated.
t.6.46.22: Indeed, Prahasta, skilled in warfare, enraged, tormented the monkeys in that supreme battle with a mighty flood of arrows.
t.6.46.23: The earth, strewn with the bodies of the monkeys and the rākṣasas, became dreadful, as though covered with fallen mountains.
t.6.46.24: That earth, covered with a flood of blood, shone forth as if overspread with flowering palāśa trees in the month of Mādhava.
t.6.46.25: A river whose banks were the heaps of slain heroes, whose great trees were the shattered weapons, whose mighty waters were the torrents of blood, and which flowed on toward the ocean of Yama.
t.6.46.26: A river whose deep mire was liver and spleen, whose moss was scattered entrails, whose fish were severed trunks and heads, and whose grassy banks were limbs and fragments of bodies.
t.6.46.27: That river was crowded with flocks of vultures and swans and frequented by herons and cranes. It was covered all over with fat for foam, and it resounded with the moans of the stricken.
t.6.46.28: That river formed of the battlefield, hard for cowards to cross, like a river at the passing of the clouds, frequented by haṃsas and sārasa cranes.
t.6.46.29: The rākṣasas and the foremost of the monkeys crossed that river, so hard to cross, just as leaders of elephant herds cross a lotus pond strewn with lotus pollen.
t.6.46.30: Then Nīla swiftly caught sight of Prahasta, stationed on his chariot, releasing floods of arrows and striking down the monkeys.
t.6.46.32: Struck by him, that bull among rākṣasas, enraged and roaring, rained showers of arrows upon the commander of the army of the monkeys.
t.6.46.31: That mighty great monkey, uprooting a tree, struck Prahasta, the supremely invincible one, as he came rushing at him.
t.6.46.33: Unable to ward it off, he received it with his eyes closed, just as a bull receives the autumn rain that has suddenly come upon it.
t.6.46.34: In just the same way, Nīla, his eyes closed, suddenly endured the unassailable and most dreadful shower of arrows from Prahasta.
t.6.46.35: Enraged by the shower of arrows, the mighty Nīla struck down with a huge sāla tree the horses of Prahasta, swift as thought.
t.6.46.36: But Prahasta, the commander of the army, made bowless by him, seized a dreadful club and leapt down from his chariot.
t.6.46.37: Those two commanders of armies, swift and mighty, their fury aroused, stood with their limbs smeared with blood, like two elephants in rut.
t.6.46.38: Tearing at each other with their very sharp fangs, the two, resembling a lion and a tiger, behaved like a lion and a tiger.
t.6.46.39: The two heroes, victorious through their valor and never turning back in battle, were eager to win glory, and they were like Vṛtra and Vāsava.
t.6.46.40: Then Prahasta, greatly enraged, struck Nīla on the forehead with his club, and blood flowed from him.
t.6.46.41: Then the great monkey, his limbs smeared with blood, seized a very large tree and in his rage hurled it at the chest of Prahasta.
t.6.46.42: Disregarding that blow, the mighty one seized a great club and rushed at the powerful monkey Nīla.
t.6.46.43: Then the great monkey, of great impetuosity, seeing him rushing toward him, enraged and of fierce speed, seized a huge rock.
t.6.46.44: On the head of Prahasta, who was eager for battle and fought with a mace in the fray, Nīla swiftly brought down a rock.
t.6.46.45: That huge and dreadful rock, hurled by the chief of the monkeys, then split Prahasta's head into many pieces.
t.6.46.46: Bereft of life, bereft of splendor, bereft of strength and bereft of his senses, he suddenly fell to the ground like a tree whose roots have been cut.
t.6.46.47: From him, whose head was split open, much blood flowed; it flowed from his body too, as a spring streams from a mountain.
t.6.46.48: When Prahasta had been slain by Nīla, that great army of dejected rākṣasas, once unshakable, went back to Laṅkā.
t.6.46.49: When the commander of the army had been slain, they could no longer hold their ground, but scattered like water that breaks apart on reaching a dam.
t.6.46.51: Then the victorious and mighty Nīla, leader of a troop, praised for the deed he himself had done, met with Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa and became filled with delight.
t.6.46.50: When that commander of the army had been slain, those rākṣasas, their resolve broken, went to the palace of the lord of the rākṣasas and sank into a brooding silence.
